The destroyer will also receive new High Efficiency Super-Capacity air conditioning plants to support its upgraded combat systems. The work marks the second phase of the Arleigh Burke-class ship’s upgrades under the Destroyer Modernization 2.0 program. The radar will be integrated with Aegis Combat System Baseline 10, while the new cooling plants will help support the combat systems’ electrical and thermal requirements. “The collective effort by all stakeholders has finally brought us to the point of execution,” said Capt. Tim Moore, program manager for DDG MOD 2.0. “Upon Depot Modernization Period completion, USS Pinckney will rejoin the Fleet equipped with the most comprehensive multi-spectral integrated sensor suite designed to maintain maritime superiority for decades to come.” Pinckney completed its earlier modernization period, designated DMP 1.5, in 2024. It became the first warship to receive the SLQ-32(V)7 Surface Electronic Warfare Improvement Program system and sponson modifications. The Navy adopted a phased installation approach, called Split Start, to build experience across its industry partners. Pinckney deployed to the Pacific and Middle East after completing the earlier work. The Navy said the deployment validated the ship’s advanced warfare capabilities in contested operational environments. title: After 40 years of ocean exploration, Pisces V will embark on its final mission at Bishop Museum - Maui Now
content: After nearly four decades of exploring the Pacific Ocean, the deep-sea submersible Pisces V is embarking on its final resting place at the Bishop Museum in Honolulu. The University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa announced it has donated the three-person research vessel to the museum, preserving its legacy of deep-ocean exploration, volcanic research and historic maritime discoveries. It is accompanied by a 35-year video and biological data archive. “The donation ensures the submersible’s storied past will be celebrated and shared with museum visitors from Hawai‘i and around the world,” said Chip Fletcher, dean of the UH Mānoa School of Ocean and Earth Science and Technology, which is home of the Hawaiʻi Undersea Research Laboratory. The laboratory operated Pisces V and its sister submersible, Pisces IV, for decades. After years in storage and no federal funding for refurbishment or redeployment, UH gifted the research vessel to the museum. UH acquired Pisces V in 1985. Throughout the Pacific basin, it ferried researchers to places no human had seen before. With its unique size, maneuverability and ability to operate at depths up to 6,500 feet, it navigated complex terrain and explored delicate ecosystems. “Operating as the only U.S. deep submergence facility based in the Pacific Rim, HURL’s work with Pisces V revolutionized oceanography across several fronts,” said Terry Kerby, veteran Pisces V pilot and laboratory operations director. The submersible enabled exploration of the seamounts and coral reefs of the Main and Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. It made more dives on Hawaiʻi’s active underwater volcano, Kamaʻehuakanaloa (previously known as Lōʻihi Seamount), than any other vessel. Throughout the Pacific basin, the submersible ferried teams of researchers on voyages of discovery to places no human had seen before. In 2005, Pisces V embarked on a five-month expedition across the Pacific, exploring active submarine volcanoes along the Kermadec Arc near New Zealand. “We discovered multiple new species and by combining submersible operations with human divers, we explored deep-sea coral ecosystems in a new way,” Kerby said. Pisces V, with Kerby at the helm, discovered the Japanese midget submarine sunk by the USS Ward hours before the attack on Pearl Harbor and massive World War II Japanese aircraft-carrying submarines off Oʻahu.“We want to make sure the important legacy of these submarines is maintained and communicated to our visitors,” said Kris Helgen, president and CEO of Bishop Museum. “The role of Bishop Museum involves telling the stories that matter to Hawai‘i and the Pacific, including stories of ocean exploration.” Haiku • Hali‘imaile • Makawao • Pukalani • Haiku • Kula

title: Triple-Black 1971 Plymouth Cuda Sells for $385K, Sets Record for V-Code Hardtops - autoevolution
content:
Specifically, the all-black Cuda you see here crossed the block for $385,000, a figure that also includes the buyer's premium. The selling price makes it the seventh most expensive vehicle auctioned off at the event. It's also the most expensive classic that's still factory stock (a 1969 Road Runner restomod fetched $407,000). Despite the high sticker, this Cuda doesn't have a 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi. However, it does have the next best thing under the hood. I'm talking about the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Six-Barrel V8, which, much like the Hemi, was discontinued after the 1971 model year. And Plymouth didn't sell many cars equipped with this engine either. Barracuda deliveries dropped to only 16,492 units in 1971. Only a quarter of these cars were high-performance Cuda models, and most of them rolled off the assembly line with the standard 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) big-block or the 340-cubic-inch (5.6-liter) small-block. The Hemi, which made the Cuda very expensive to insure, found its way into only 114 cars. The 440 Six-Barrel wasn't notably more popular either; only 254 customers opted for this powerplant. This Cuda is one of those cars, sporting the correct V code in the VIN sequence. But the production number is actually much lower. It's all due to the four-speed manual gearbox, which was paired with only 113 Six-Barrel engines. Five of these cars were convertibles, so we're looking at one of only 108 hardtops fitted with this drivetrain combo. I could also factor in the triple-black color combo, but I don't have specific production figures to run by. But I do know that black wasn't a popular choice at the time, and I'm willing to bet that fewer than 10 cars were ordered with this exact color/drivetrain setup. Oh, did I also mention that it's a Super Track Pak car? This means that the 390-horsepower V8 mates with a Dana 60 rear axle with 4.10 gears. In short, this Mopar will be at home on the drag strip if you're into quarter-mile runs. As expected from a classic that sold for over $300,000, this Cuda has a numbers-matching drivetrain. It also shows only 34,349 miles (55,279 km) on the odometer and comes with the original broadcast sheet. The selling price sets a new benchmark for V-code hardtops. At $385,000, this Cuda outsold a different four-speed Six-Barrel example that went under the hammer for $363,000 earlier in 2026. However, it's not the most expensive 1971 V-code Cuda, as a convertible changed hands for $1.15 million, while a second one traded for $962,500. Speaking of million-dollar cars, Dallas/Fort Worth 2026 saw a 2006 Ford GT Heritage Edition top the sales chart with a $1.67 million sticker. The top three was completed by a 2026 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1X Stars & Steel Edition ($550,000) and a 2027 Corvette ZR1X 3LZ Convertible ($495,000). When you think about those who made it out of the neighborhood and into the more affluent parts of your home, you think of them in a Caddy. The Escalade became the harbinger of wealth when it became the status symbol of the urban and hip hop cultures. Now the Escalade is the vessel Cadillac is using to celebrate 125 years with the Escalade-V. "Every soul deserves a shot at a Cadillac, but not everyone should be guaranteed a Cadillac." — Ben Stein This is the first in a collector's series celebrating over a century of iconic luxury. The new Escalade-V comes with a slew of features. The most unique and one I would show off at every turn is the custom VIN. "From its exclusive design to its highly limited availability, this special edition gives collectors a distinctive way to celebrate Cadillac's legacy while looking ahead to its future." title: Colts Jonathan Taylor finally scores on long touchdown run v. Vikings - Yahoo Sports
content: The Indianapolis Colts are looking to pull off an upset against the Minnesota Vikings, and while there is still a way to go in this game, they're off to a good start. The Colts started off well on defense by stopping the Vikings on fourth and one in Indianapolis' territory. Their offense also began strong, going down the field on a seven-play touchdown drive on their opening possession. They converted two third downs on this drive before running back Jonathan Taylor broke loose for a 38-yard touchdown, which gave the Colts a 7-0 lead. Here is a look at Taylor's touchdown, courtesy of the Indianapolis Colts' official social media: Jonathan Taylor breaks through!📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/lcFr4An7JV This touchdown run is also a good sign for Taylor, who has struggled to generate those home run plays this season. His longest run of the year in the first six weeks was a 24-yard run, and he is averaging a career-low of four yards per carry. If the Colts can get Taylor going, perhaps they can pull off this upset and string some wins together in the second half of the season. title: Liverpool Player Ratings v Brighton: Araujo Dominates & Isak Scores In Home Win - Yahoo Sports
content: Liverpool made it four wins in a row, as they dispatched Brighton by two goals to nil, thanks to a goal from Alexander Isak, as well as an unfortunate own goal from Pascal Groß. It was Andoni Iraola's first win at Anfield in the league, and he hopes it is the first of many. Here are our player ratings (out of 10) following this big victory at Anfield. A clean sheet with not a lot to do, which is a perfect day for the Brazilian shot stopper. Dealt with the threat posed on the left-hand side, and linked up well with the winger in front of him, whether that was Gakpo or Barcola. A much more composed and reliable performance today from the skipper, who dealt with everything in the air and covered well when Kerkez was left under pressure. Another strong showing from Jacquet today, a heroic piece of defending in the first half, helping keep a valuable clean sheet. His determination made the first goal for LFC, hustling the Brighton defence, winning the ball back and delivering a dangerous ball into the box. He was also strong defensively, even clearing danger with his head while on the ground, another top draw display from the Uruguayan. Positionally superb today, was in the right place at the right time to clear any danger lurking around the Reds penalty area. A few neat turns in the middle of the pitch, but it was a quiet game overall from Ryan Gravenberch. A peach of a ball into the box that allowed Isak to convert, and while most of Liverpool's attacks came from the other side, he was a threat whenever he got on the ball. Took the shot, that was deflected into the back of the net by Pascal Groß, hopefully the knock he picked up isn't too serious. A constant threat on the counter, but his decision making was poor throughout the game. Took his goal really well, a striker's finish from Liverpool's number nine, exactly what he is in the team for. Came off the bench and made a crucial tackle immediately. Had a couple of his signature runs down the right-hand side to relieve the pressure off the Reds' backline. Pressed from the front superbly, but didn't have much service for the short time he was on the field. He was a crucial part of the opener, with his endeavour and determination to win the ball back, leading to the Uruguayan managing to get a cross into the box, which Wirtz directed into the path of Pascal Groß, who hit it past Verbruggen for an own goal. Then, in the second half, the Reds' defensive credentials were tested, but Ronald Araujo stood out massively. After an up-and-down game against Villarreal, he bounced back against Brighton with several clean, but thunderous, challenges that not only got the crowd off their feet, but ensured that a high-scoring Brighton side couldn't find a way through.

title: Isak, Barcola and Wirtz turn up - player ratings for Liverpool v Brighton - BBC
content: Liverpool earn first league win at Anfield with victory over Brighton Liverpool beat Brighton 2-0 at Anfield with Alexander Isak scoring the second goal, four minutes after Pascal Gross' own-goal gave the home side the lead. Here's how I rated the players and how you rated the players. Alisson: Didn't have a save to make in the first half but was nearly punished when Yasin Ayari hit the post after his careless pass out from the back. Will be delighted with the clean sheet. 7 Ronald Araujo: Showed great strength in the build-up for the first goal and was solid again, defensively. Nearly scored too but his effort was saved. 7 Jeremy Jacquet: Another good performance. Composed on the ball and made some crucial blocks. 7 Virgil van Dijk: Back to his usual self after a relatively poor display in midweek. Another clean sheet in the Premier League. 7 Milos Kerkez: Didn't have the best of games and had his work cut out against Diego Gomez, but ultimately was part of a Liverpool backline that kept Brighton out. 6 Ryan Gravenberch: Solid work rate, particularly in a game where Liverpool had a lot less of the ball. 7 Alexis Mac Allister: Certainly one of Liverpool's better players this season and bar some loose passes, this was another encouraging display from the Argentine. 7 Bradley Barcola: Did superbly to tee up Isak and was a handful all afternoon for Olivier Boscagli. Did everything but score. 8 Florian Wirtz: Played with confidence and didn't hold back with the strike that resulted in an own goal from Gross. Caused Brighton plenty of problems throughout. Went off shortly after receiving treatment. 8 Cody Gakpo: Constantly threatened, playing down his preferred left, and had two efforts saved. Unlucky not to get an assist too. 7 Alexander Isak: A simple finish but in the right place at the right time for his sixth Premier League goal in as many games. Still not at his best yet but with those numbers, Andoni Iraola will be delighted. 7 Nyoni (on 65, Wirtz): Solid challenge instantly after coming on and the teenager looks like he is improving every week. 7 Subs not used: Mamardashvili, Gomez, Endo, Chiesa, McConnell. 'Scary for the rest of the league' - Williams impressed by Liverpool Bart Verbruggen: Made some good saves in the first half but was undone by the deflection for the first goal and had no chance for Isak's strike. 5 Ferdi Kadioglu: Forced off with an injury in the sixth minute. Was holding his hip as he came off. 5 Luka Vuskovic: Part of a back line that conceded in the league for the first time since 16 September, but the 19-year-old looked good on the ball. 6 Lewis Dunk: Like Vuskovic, battled well but the Brighton back line were punished by Liverpool's ruthlessness. 5 Olivier Boscagli: Lost the ball for Liverpool's second goal and struggled to deal with Barcola. Booked for a foul on Barcola just before half-time and replaced at the break. 4 Pascal Gross: Should have got an assist when he teed up Ayari but did not cover himself in glory when his clearance landed at Wirtz's feet and the subsequent strike deflected off Gross and ended up in the back of the net. 5 Chema Andres: Was good on the ball and tidy in possession but took a knock and was replaced early on in the second half. 6 Diego Gomez: Played a lovely through ball to Gross for Ayari's chance and linked up really well with Joao Costinha. 7 Yasin Ayari: Missed a huge chance when the game was 0-0 and his side were punished shortly after, then hit the post with a good effort in the first half. 6 Maxim de Cuyper: Had a quiet first half and dropped into left-back for the second half after Jack Hinshelwood came on for Boscagli. 5 Charalampos Kostoulas: Got on the ball plenty and always offered an option but did not do enough to truly threaten Alisson. 6 Costinha (on 6, Kadioglu): Thrown in early on and linked well with Gomez going forward but struggled to contain Gakpo. 6 Hinshelwood (on 46, Boscagli): Did well after coming on but could not get Brighton back in the game. 6 Yalcouye (on 54, Andres): Did not get on the ball enough after coming on. 5 Subs not used: Steele, Hadjam, Rutter, David, Osman, O'Riley. title: Holy Flip, It’s a Cadillac CT6-V With the Blackwing V8 for Sale - The Drive
content:
Published				

					Oct 25, 2026 11:00 AM EDT The Daily Brief wraps up the biggest stories and our exclusive reporting on the auto industry and car culture. No automaker pulls the plug on exciting projects like General Motors. The more ambitious the engineering, the more likely it is to be killed off after a very short production run. Sometimes this is intentional; the C4 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1 was always meant to be a low-volume version of a car that was on its way out. But more often, GM hypes something new and different only to pull it from the market a few years later. Just look at the Chevy Volt, or the car that originated the Blackwing name at Cadillac. Before Blackwing was a trim level, it was an engine. And it powered the performance version of the Cadillac CT6, itself a highly ambitious attempt to elevate the brand to higher levels of luxury and match the Germans in engineering sophistication. But the Cadillac CT6-V, powered by the Blackwing V8, is a rare bird, with just under 1,000 reportedly produced. One of them is up for sale on Cars & Bids. The CT6 was introduced for the 2016 model year as a more upmarket sedan sitting above the CTS and ATS, and with modern technology to banish all memories of the retirement-community-special XTS. It was built on a new platform mixing steel and aluminum, which was designed from the start to accommodate the 34 speakers of the optional Bose Panaray audio system. The CT6 was also the first car to get GM’s Super Cruise hands-free driving system, and while lower trim levels had pedestrian powertrains, a twin-turbo 3.0-liter V6 and a plug-in hybrid powertrain with Volt-derived components were on offer. A 2019 facelift upped the ante with the Blackwing engine: a twin-turbo, 4.2-liter V8 designed to go up against the best from Germany. A detuned version was shoved into the CT6 Platinum trim level, while the CT6-V got a high-output version making 550 horsepower and 640 pound-feet of torque. The Blackwing engine was harnessed to a 10-speed automatic transmission and all-wheel drive. By the time the Blackwing-powered models were ready to go on sale, GM was already preparing to cancel the CT6. Just 915 CT6-V and 285 CT6 Platinum models with the V8 were produced, as 2019 and 2020 models. GM canceled the CT6 at a time when it was culling most of its sedans and hatchbacks to free up production capacity for more profitable SUVs and pickup trucks as the automaker prepared to invest heavily in electrification. But GM also ruled out using the Blackwing engine in other models. The complex engine was more expensive to produce and unique to Cadillac, unlike GM’s simpler small-block V8s. It probably didn’t help that the engine was a passion project of then-Cadillac boss Johan de Nysschen, whose departure left it without a champion. Cadillac eventually repurposed the Blackwing name for its industrial-strength performance models, but there will never be another V-Series model like the CT6-V. Showing 49,800 miles with some chips, scratches, and scuffs, this one can be yours for a fraction of its original price. The high bid was just under $25,000 at the time of writing. title: El clásico today: How to watch Barcelona v Real Madrid, TV channels & live stream Sunday 25 October - The Guardian
content: How will Barcelona and Real Madrid fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options El clásico remains one of the most important fixtures in world soccer, with Sunday’s encounter at the Camp Nou highly anticipated as a fixture that could set the tone for the rest of the La Liga season. Domestically, Barcelona are in frightening form. While the Catalans were humbled by Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League, they are setting a perfect pace at the top of La Liga having won all nine of their fixtures so far, scoring a ridiculous 39 goals in the process. Real Madrid, meanwhile, have scored eight goals in their last two games. José Mourinho has struggled to find the right balance in his team since returning to the Santiago Bernabéu, but Los Blancos may have peaked at the right time to take on their fiercest rivals. Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s La Liga fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks and online streaming options. Watching Barcelona is a good time. That has been the case in all three of Flick’s seasons in charge of the Catalan side, but the dial has been turned even higher this season, illustrated by Barça’s tally of 50 goals in 12 games in all competitions. Barcelona’s high defensive line remains the weak spot, but that same line makes their high-risk, high-energy approach possible. The high-wire act has made Barça the most watchable team in Europe. Real Madrid have the talent to go toe-to-toe with Barcelona, but perhaps not the cohesion and structure to sustain a performance for 90 minutes. The visitors’ best opportunities will surely come on the counterattack where they carry real threat. Player to watch: Lamine Yamal, Barcelona – The day before the teenager’s potential crowning as a Ballon d’Or winner, Yamal has the opportunity to prove why he is the best player in the world. The 19-year-old could dominate Sunday’s match.

title: The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle - The Guardian
content: The AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting back Dale Johnston opens the gate to his neat suburban garden on the western fringes of Newport in South Wales. There’s a trampoline and a slide on the lawn for his grandchildren, and chairs for him and his wife. He should be enjoying the light draining from the perfect autumnal sky – but almost his entire view is blotted out by a vast expanse of prefabricated panels. The 23 metre-high grey hulk looming over him and his neighbours is a hyperscale datacentre. It is heralded by the area’s Labour politicians as a job creator, yet all Johnston can think about is what he has lost: “Before, the sun used to come around here and it was lovely.” The way residents have been treated is “disgusting”. Johnston, who used to work for a chemical company in the city, worries what their lives will be like when the centre is switched on: the 36 sets of air blast coolers, needed to stop the chips inside overheating, most likely generate a constant drone, while regular testing of 60 back-up diesel generators, to prevent costly interruption to the flow of data, could produce harmful fumes. He already has to keep his bathroom window closed to stop the low hum from another facility on the rapidly expanding 46-acre datacentre campus that borders the small enclave of 27 houses. His wife, a nurse who works night shifts, can barely sleep already. He shakes his head in despair: “We just don’t know what’s going to happen.” Johnston can talk about little else, but he feels no one in authority is listening. He’s invited councillors and MPs backing the development to visit his garden. But “they won’t come around here to see what they’ve done”. This is the frontline of Britain’s datacentre boom, which is pitting residents against giant US tech firms seeking to build a network of facilities capable of providing the immense computing muscle for powerful AI models. There are 315 hyperscale datacentres waiting to connect to the national grid, which carries electricity from power plants to homes and businesses (hyperscale typically means facilities with at least 5,000 servers and 10,000 sq ft in size). Combined, these new centres will require 73GW of power, 28GW higher than the typical peak energy demand of 45GW on a cold winter’s day. Wales is one of the main development hotspots outside London. It already has the largest datacentre capacity beyond the capital, with new hyperscale facilities planned for former industrial and urban sites. The Keir Starmer-led Labour government viewed this as an inevitable revolution, which the country must embrace or be left behind. It established five AI growth zones to push more datacentres through the planning system and speed up connections to the national grid. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has signalled little will change, turning down calls for a moratorium and insisting datacentres bring economic benefits. But anti-datacentre groups springing up in villages, towns and cities across the country see it rather differently: as the imposition of a resource-hungry, polluting industry that increases profits for often US big tech, with little tangible benefit to local people or the country as a whole. Digital storage is nothing new. The first home PC users saved files on floppy discs and hard drives; businesses used their own server rooms in the 80s and 90s, then moved to off-site facilities as their needs grew. But the development of cloud computing services in the 2010s, such as Google Drive, and AI chatbots in the 2020s, like ChatGPT, led to even greater information and processing demands, which the tech industry insists can only be met by larger and larger datacentres. This has driven huge speculative bets on hyperscale hubs, which investors and tech firms hope will one day reap the rewards of an AI-led transformation of the economy. Globally, it is estimated spending on new facilities could reach $7tn by 2030 – more than double the cost of the New Deal, the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe after the second world war and the Apollo space programme combined, even allowing for inflation. The US is at the forefront of the boom, already hosting roughly half of the world’s hyperscale capacity. But the industry is facing a furious backlash, with three-quarters of Americans now opposed to datacentre development and blaming it for increasing energy bills, threatening water supplies in drought-hit areas and spewing out toxic fumes. More than 500 counties and municipalities have passed permanent or temporary datacentre bans. Loudoun County in northern Virginia sits in what is known as Data Center Alley because it is home to more facilities than anywhere else in the world. Greg Pirio’s life was turned upside down when a gas-powered datacentre opened 150 metres from his home last year. “This neighbourhood was calm and peaceful, and it’s turned into this nightmare,” he says on a video call. “Our quality of life has been degraded so much.” The noise from the centre’s eight gas turbines is “like being at an airport with all these engines roaring,” Pirio says. “It has given many of my neighbours headaches. It has kept children up at night.” Pirio, who used to work for the Voice of America radio station, has also developed health problems since it opened, including dry eyes and chest tightness. Once he had to leave his house because he was struggling to breathe: “I know whenever the diesel generators are on, because I feel it in my lungs.” The UK has not yet seen the same level of opposition as the US. But anti-datacentre groups are gathering momentum. Residents in east London are waging a high-profile campaign against a new datacentre on Brick Lane, including protesting outside the offices of Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, who overturned a council decision blocking the scheme. Seasoned campaigner Owen Espley, who works for environmental charity Global Action Plan, is helping scores of residents’ groups organise against planned datacentres. “This summer has been wild. Every other week a new group has popped up. Petitions are getting thousands of signatures in days,” he says. “Communities are in uproar, and most politicians are playing catch-up.” Espley has been taken aback by the gulf between the government’s conviction that there is no alternative and ordinary people’s deepening understanding of the complex issues at stake. “There has been a real grassroots questioning of datacentres that connects British Bangladeshis in Brick Lane with Hertfordshire villagers and communities in Northumberland, who want good jobs to come back,” he says. “It is astounding.” In fact, there are many alternative pathways to market-­led expansion – from tougher regulation to prioritising publicly-owned data infrastructure – which serve communal goals, such as the heart disease and dementia research powered by Bristol University’s new Isambard-AI facility. “First, we need strong standards for private datacentres,” Espley says. “Second, we need industrial strategy to deliver our own public computer, rather than an assumption that US big tech building and owning everything is the only way forward.” On the deprived eastern edges of Cardiff, the early morning sunshine is warming a car park dotted with scraggly weeds. The perimeter fence is overgrown with brambles, with patches of singed, blackened grass from a recent wildfire visible just beyond. It looks abandoned but soon cars carrying doctors, nurses and other NHS staff start arriving. They are here to catch free buses to Cardiff’s Heath hospital, the largest in Wales. Hundreds are said to use the park and ride every day, but it is under threat because Labour-controlled Cardiff council wants to sell the land to a property developer, Curtis Hall, to build a hyperscale data facility. The centre will use up to 150 megawatts (MW) of electricity a year, more than triple the demand of a city the size of Cardiff. The development is one of the most controversial in Wales. Council meetings have been disrupted and more than 1,200 planning objections lodged. Last month, the new Plaid Cymru-led government ordered the council to put the application on hold while it considered whether to take the decision out of councillors’ hands. Campaigners are determined to keep up the pressure on the Welsh government. Sue Elias, a retired librarian with seemingly endless reserves of energy, dashes back and forth reattaching her “Ditch the datacentre” banner to the car park fence and taping leaflets to the bus stop glass. “What is going to happen to all the people who use the park and ride? It’s bonkers,” she says. Elias has leafleted the park and ride every Wednesday morning for six weeks. Today she is collecting signatures for an open letter to prove it is well used – so far she has added the names of 1,300 staff and patients. “I’ve not done anything like this before but I’m told I’m a natural,” she says with a mischievous smile, before breaking off to speak to staff arriving for the next bus. She belongs to community-based union Acorn, which has campaigned against the scheme, and has taken part in protests, including bursting into a council planning meeting in July. “We’d sent emails, done petitions, but we’d had nothing back – tumbleweed. They’re our elected representatives … They should be talking with us.” It is hard to find anyone in support of the plan in the queue for the bus, which runs three times an hour. “I use it every day. Without it, I probably wouldn’t continue working at the hospital,” says Ami George, a midwife. “Parking there causes that much stress.” Across Cardiff’s Rhymney River, which curves around the proposed datacentre development, the area’s newest residents have only recently moved into 100 homes built under the city council’s flagship house-building programme. Nick Richards, a freelance filmmaker and skateboarder, and his wife arrived in November. “It felt like the stars had aligned because there is a brand new skate park up the road … the best in Cardiff. It’s amazing,” he says. “I never pictured myself living in suburbia but when we came we saw kids playing outside and thought, this is a really nice area.” Like many other residents on the estate, Richards had no idea the council was planning to sell the park and ride to a datacentre developer. They moved in two months before the planning application was submitted. Instead of enjoying their new life, they now fear they will never be able to sell. Their home is 300 metres from what the plans describe as the temporary energy centre, which includes seven giant gas turbines. They are expected to power the facility around the clock for five years, according to documents filed by the developer. “I feel trapped,” Richards says, pacing his kitchen. “I couldn’t look prospective buyers in the eye and not say there’s going to be seven gas turbines right next to them.” Richards has pored over the planning documents and leafleted every house on the new estate, including a care home, which will be just 150 metres from the turbines. “This datacentre will be powered by gas turbines,” he says. “They will pump nitrogen dioxide into our atmosphere. There will also be fine particulate matter and formaldehyde. All these toxins cause health conditions, such as asthma, COPD and heart disease.” Air quality assessments commissioned by the developer estimate the emissions will be within safe levels. Curtis Hall says the scheme cannot proceed without 100% compliance with all environmental and public health regulatory requirements. The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend. There are more than 100 other planned UK datacentres aiming to use gas turbines due to the long wait to be connected to the grid. Richards doesn’t want his estate to be a test case. “Within a mile of this datacentre are 30,000 people. But the people building this centre don’t live here ... They don’t give two shits about Welsh people.” A stone’s throw away is Llanrumney Hall, once the home of privateer and slave trader Sir Henry Morgan, who gave his name to Captain Morgan rum. It is now a thriving community centre, with a cafe, recording studio and creche. Labour councillor Lee Bridgeman is vaping on an outdoor table, dressed in a hoodie and baseball cap. He ran the local youth centre until it was lost to austerity-era cuts, and though he’s a high-ranking councillor, jointly responsible for housing and communities, he does regular youth work shifts in the area, one of the poorest in Cardiff. “Llanrumney runs through my veins,” he says. “I’m not your usual politician. I don’t go to conferences. I got into politics to help the community.” Bridgeman is charming and friendly – but he is not afraid of a fight. He is one of the few public figures in the area who has spoken out in support of the development, sometimes clashing with anti-datacentre campaigners on local Facebook groups. “Some of the information being spread is scaremongering,” he says. “They are telling residents their electricity bills will go up … the river and reservoir will be drained … It’s false information.” Many of these fears stem from the US, where the rapid expansion of hyperscale facilities has been linked to rising electricity bills, water shortages and toxic air pollution. Bridgeman argues that “planning processes are totally different in the UK. So whereas [US authorities] turn a blind eye to some of the environmental impacts of those monstrosities, that would never happen in the UK.” He “wouldn’t be comfortable” if the gas turbines were running for five years but thinks they might not be needed if the datacentre can connect to the grid sooner. The backlash has caught him by surprise, but he blames outside activists. “I didn’t see it coming. I didn’t think there would be this much interference,” he says. Emotions are running high in the city. Some residents say they have been blocked by councillors when trying to question them on Facebook. Planning committee members have received threatening emails, Bridgeman says. “Threats like ‘I will come after you ... we will make your life hell.’ That shouldn’t happen.” Although the datacentre will employ only up to 125 people when it is built, Bridgeman believes it could encourage other big companies to east Cardiff: “I’m told the knock-on effect could lead to thousands of jobs.” Later that day, residents squeeze into the local boxing club for a public meeting about the datacentre plan. It is standing room only, with people lining the walls. Bridgeman repeats his claim that few locals have complained: “I have hundreds of emails from residents ... So far I’ve had two emails with regards to the datacentre.” Some in the audience react angrily. There are shouts of, “We don’t know you, that’s why” and, “Have you heard of social media?” One woman stands up and says, “Don’t tell me you haven’t been privy to the meetings … or things online.” In a show of hands, roughly three-quarters of the 80 to 100 people in the room indicate they are from Llanrumney, almost all opposed. There are cries of, “There you are … you don’t need emails!” and, “That’s every person!” Almost three weeks later, Bridgeman performs a sudden about-turn, submitting a formal letter of objection to the scheme, noting that he has heard from a large number of residents. The UK hyperscale buildout has been focused on London, but datacentre developers are increasingly targeting areas outside the south-east, to escape severe electrical grid capacity limits. Wales already has the largest datacentre capacity of anywhere outside the capital. Many more could be coming: five of Wales’s largest new and proposed datacentres will consume more electricity than all Welsh homes put together. While the previous Welsh Labour administration welcomed the building spree, claiming giant tech firms’ investment would generate thousands of jobs, the Plaid Cymru-led government has been more circumspect, with ministers emphasising it must benefit Wales. In the light and airy Welsh parliament building, which overlooks Cardiff Bay, opposition is growing. Plaid Cymru’s Nick Carter, who is the Senedd member for Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, which includes Cardiff East, worries that the surging market will benefit developers and US tech firms rather than the public. “As a party, we’re not going to want to see a proliferation of datacentres, haphazardly being built across the country, on what may be an opportunistic basis,” he says. Carter, who has a background in commercial property, has examined the Cardiff plans in detail. He says the developer, Curtis Hall, has no track record in datacentres; “They could be a front for someone else: Google, Microsoft, whoever. I can understand why these operators need datacentres, but I’m not sure members of the public share the need.” In response, Curtis Hall says it never claimed it would operate the facility itself, adding it had been working on datacentre projects for five years. Carter is glad the Welsh government has intervened in Cardiff. But he doesn’t believe Wales needs to follow Scotland by imposing a moratorium on new datacentres: “The Welsh government is developing a strategy for datacentres nationally. We’ll see what comes out of that.” However, it is not clear how the Welsh government can meet its goal to reach net zero by 2040 without limiting datacentre expansion. Carter admits, “It’s massively problematic.” In Westminster, similar questions have been asked. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology tells me the government will enable the development of datacentres by generating unprecedented amounts of clean power. A soft autumnal dusk descends on the residents living beside the new datacentre in Newport. Its sleek industrial-grey walls cast shadows across the closest gardens and homes. Much of the anger and frustration that met the original proposals has given way to weariness and resignation. Some residents talk of moving away, while others are mollified by meetings with the US-based data campus operator, Vantage. Yet their troubles may only just be beginning – right now, only one of the three Vantage datacentres is operational. Microsoft will be opening its own nearby soon. When all are running, there could be upwards of 500 air handling units working at the same time, with back-up diesel generators needing regular testing, so they can immediately fire up if there is a power cut. Newport council’s chief scientific officer warned during the planning process that the fumes from all the generators had the “potential to cause unacceptable air pollution levels under use, and testing needs to be understood and mitigation proposed, if needed”. The council tells me it doesn’t have a duty to monitor emissions from generators, but says its officers check air quality management plans, and ask managers to minimise the impact of generator tests. Vantage says all its facilities operate in accordance with noise and air quality controls. It says it will monitor impacts and investigate concerns when the new centre opens. Some residents have already given up on democratic process. Johnston fought the proposals through the planning process but felt he was ignored. “We’ve been let down by all of them. I’ve had electoral roll cards come through my door. But I’m voting for none of them … I can’t trust them. They don’t care about any of us.” Over the road are older homes, where staff working on a nearby wealthy estate once lived. Sonia Thomas, a retired teacher, has lived in the same housekeeper’s cottage since 1969. She can remember when orchards and fields fanned out in front of their gardens but now she doesn’t even know if the sun is shining. “From inside you see grey, not blue,” she says, glancing at the datacentre filling the sky. “It’s horrible.”

title: Confirmed Hull City v Brentford team news: Andrews makes three changes - Brentford FC
content:

title: Stevie Wonder’s greatest? It’s ‘Superstition’ v. ‘Sunshine of My Life’ - Detroit Free Press
content: What percentage of the vote did 'Superstition' receive in the semifinals? Which other songs from 'Talking Book' made the bracket? Why is the 'Talking Book' album significant in this contest? What’s the greatest Stevie Wonder song? After a month of public voting, the championship round has arrived. “Superstition” and “You Are the Sunshine of My Life” are the final contenders in a 64-song tournament loaded with classics by the iconic Motown star. Vote below to help crown the winner. Voting runs through 5 p.m. Wednesday, Oct. 28. Both finalists hail from 1972’s beloved “Talking Book,” the album that earned Wonder three Grammy Awards on his way to a career tally of 25, setting a record for a male pop artist. Here’s how the two songs advanced from the bracket’s semifinal round: No. 1 seed “Superstition” topped 1976’s “Isn’t She Lovely,” a No. 2 seed, with 65% of the vote. In a tighter matchup, No. 2 seed “You Are the Sunshine of My Life" bested 1968’s “For Once in My Life,” a No. 3 seed, with 54%. If your personal Stevie Wonder fave didn’t make it this far, take heart: With this collection of classic music, every song is a winner.
